03 — Investing

From first principles.

Simple first. Open any line for the deeper version.

The foundations

EDUCATION
You own a claim on future profits. Price = what others will pay for that claim today.
Its value is the cash it can return to owners over its whole life.
The market's price tag on the whole company. Compare companies by market cap, never by share price.
Growth in revenue matters only if it eventually becomes profit.
Gross → operating → net profit, each removing more costs.
Buybacks raise EPS without the business growing — check both.
What you pay per $1 of profit. A 25 P/E means a 4% earnings yield.
The cash that can actually be returned to owners. Harder to manipulate than earnings.
Debt amplifies outcomes. In a downturn, lenders get paid first — shareholders can be wiped out.
High and stable margins usually signal pricing power.
The single best quality measure: how much profit each dollar reinvested earns. ROIC above cost of capital (~8–10%) creates value.
Great company + bad price can be a bad investment. Expected return = yield + growth ± change in multiple.
Growth is worth more when ROIC is high and runway long.
Sources: network effects, switching costs, scale, brands, patents, regulation.
Moats are the long-lived version; advantages can be temporary.
Earnings, products, regulation, spin-offs. Catalysts put a clock on a thesis.
Volatility is the price of admission; permanent loss is what to avoid.
10 AI stocks are one bet. Correlation, not count, is what matters.
A 20% chance of 5× and 80% chance of −50% has EV +20% — but you may not survive the losses. Size for survival.

Ways to invest

Buy assets below intrinsic value.

Why it can work
Investors overreact to bad news; mean reversion in fundamentals and multiples.
When it works
After panics; when rates fall; when cheap stocks are not value traps.
When it fails
Value traps; technology disruption; long periods (2010–2020) when growth dominates.
Main risk
Paying a low price for a declining business.

Own companies growing fast for a long time.

Why it can work
Compounding of revenue and profit outruns any starting valuation.
When it works
Low rates, new tech cycles.
When it fails
Rising rates; growth decelerates while priced for perfection (2000, 2022).
Main risk
Multiple compression.

Own high-ROIC, low-debt, steady businesses.

Why it can work
Markets underprice persistence of high profitability.
When it works
Recessions and slow markets.
When it fails
Junk rallies; when quality becomes expensive.
Main risk
Overpaying for safety.

Buy recent winners, avoid losers.

Why it can work
Under-reaction to news, herding, slow capital flows.
When it works
Trending markets.
When it fails
Sharp reversals after bear-market bottoms (2009 momentum crash).
Main risk
Crashes; high turnover.

Systematically tilt toward rewarded traits (value, momentum, quality, size, low vol).

Why it can work
Risk premia or persistent behavioral errors.
When it works
Over long horizons, diversified across factors.
When it fails
Factors can underperform for a decade; crowding.
Main risk
Long droughts; data-mined factors.

Buy what's hated.

Why it can work
Sentiment extremes overshoot.
When it works
Capitulation moments.
When it fails
When the bad news is correct.
Main risk
Catching falling knives.

Spin-offs, restructurings, mergers, buybacks.

Why it can work
Forced sellers and complexity create mispricing.
When it works
Any market; low correlation.
When it fails
Deals break; complexity hides risk.
Main risk
Event risk.

Trade around defined events (earnings, approvals, deals).

Why it can work
Market misprices event probabilities.
When it works
High-dispersion markets.
When it fails
Binary outcomes go wrong.
Main risk
Binary loss.

Hold great businesses for decades.

Why it can work
Time × ROIC × reinvestment; low taxes and costs.
When it works
Always — if you can hold.
When it fails
If you sell in panics or the moat erodes.
Main risk
Behavioral — not holding.

Invest in a structural trend (AI, electrification).

Why it can work
Big shifts create big winners.
When it works
Early in a cycle.
When it fails
Theme right, stocks wrong (dot-com).
Main risk
Paying for the theme twice.

Position based on rates, inflation, growth, currencies.

Why it can work
Macro drives cross-asset returns.
When it works
Regime changes (2022).
When it fails
Macro is hard to forecast and timing is everything.
Main risk
Being early = being wrong.

Small positions with large possible payoffs.

Why it can work
Markets underprice convex outcomes sometimes.
When it works
When sized small and diversified.
When it fails
When positions are oversized.
Main risk
Most options expire worthless.

What it takes to 2×, 3×, 5×, 10×

EDUCATION

Return multiple = (Revenue_end/Revenue_start) × (Margin_end/Margin_start) × (Multiple_end/Multiple_start) × (Shares_start/Shares_end). Every 10× needs several of these to move at once.

2×
≈ 26%/yr over 3 yrs · 15%/yr over 5

Revenue +50–70% with flat multiple, or steady growth + modest re-rating. Achievable for quality growth.

High expected return
3×
≈ 44%/yr over 3 yrs · 25%/yr over 5

Revenue roughly doubles AND margins expand or multiple rises. Requires a real inflection.

High expected return / high volatility
5×
≈ 71%/yr over 3 yrs · 38%/yr over 5

Revenue 3× plus profitability inflection; usually a small/mid cap (<$30B) at the start.

Speculation
10×
≈ 115%/yr over 3 yrs · 58%/yr over 5

A new market or category win: revenue 5–10× AND a re-rating. Base rates are low; most candidates fall 70%+ along the way.

06 — Swing Trading

Days to weeks.

What moves prices over a few weeks — and which classic rules survive contact with out-of-sample data.

EDUCATION
What swing trading is

Holding positions for days to weeks to capture a 'swing' in price.

Time horizon

2 days – 8 weeks. Long enough to avoid intraday noise, short enough for frequent decisions.

Trend

Higher highs and higher lows. Trade with it — the base rate is on your side.

Momentum

Speed of the move. Strong momentum tends to persist briefly, then fade.

Support / resistance

Price zones where buying or selling previously overwhelmed the other side.

Volume

Participation. Breakouts on heavy volume are more credible (not testable in FLOW's data).

Breakouts

Price leaves a range. Most fail; the few that work run far — low win rate, high payoff.

Pullbacks

Temporary dips inside an uptrend. High win rate, small wins — vulnerable to regime shifts.

Moving averages

20/50/200-day trend filters. Simple, robust, laggy.

Relative strength

Prefer what's outperforming its benchmark.

Volatility

Wider stops in volatile markets; smaller size to keep risk constant.

Earnings catalysts

Gaps around earnings can jump stops — reduce size or avoid holding through.

Market structure

Most stocks follow the index. Fighting a falling market lowers win rates.

Risk/reward

Target at least 2:1 reward-to-risk, or a high win rate if lower.

Trade invalidation

Decide before entry what price proves you wrong.

Position sizing

Risk 0.5–1% of the paper account per trade.

Drawdowns

Losing streaks of 6–10 trades happen even with an edge. Size so they're survivable.

Strategy experiments

07 — Quant Trading

Measure everything.

The vocabulary of quantitative trading, then a playground running on 126 years of real S&P 500 data — in your browser.

EDUCATION
Simple return r = P1/P0 − 1. Multiply (1+r) across periods to compound.
They add across time, which makes math easier. ≈ simple return for small moves.
Monthly σ × √12, daily σ × √252. The S&P 500 has run ≈15–16% per year since 1900.
Diversification works when correlations are low — and they rise in crises.
Drives portfolio variance: σp² = wᵀΣw.
Cross-sectional (winners vs losers) and time-series (asset vs its own past).
Works at short horizons in some assets; FLOW's index test failed out of sample.
A slow average is a crude trend detector. Price above = trend up.
Rotate toward stronger assets.
β = cov(r, m)/var(m). β 1.5 moves ~1.5× the market.
Most 'alpha' disappears after costs and correct benchmarks.
Market, size, value, momentum, quality, low volatility.
(R − Rf)/σ. 0.5 ≈ stock market long-run; >1 sustained is rare.
Only penalizes bad volatility.
The number that decides whether you'll actually stick with a strategy. S&P 1929–32: −81%.
Needs low costs, fast execution, and leverage — institutional territory.
Requires short selling (account permissions). Relationships break.
Strategies that work in one regime often fail in another.
Necessary, never sufficient.
Test many ideas → the best one is lucky. Use out-of-sample data and simple rules.
Example: trading on a month's close at that month's start. FLOW shifts all signals one period.
Today's index members excluded the failures — inflates returns.
FLOW charges 10 bps/switch (index) and 5 bps/side (swing).
Grows with size and volatility.
Risk per trade (e.g., 1% of capital) ÷ distance to stop = position size.

Trend following

Trend following (10-month SMA)

Hold equities when the market is above its long-term average; otherwise T-bills. Hypothesis: Bear markets tend to start below a slow moving average; stepping aside cuts the deepest drawdowns.

  • →Hold S&P 500 when month-end price > 10-month SMA
  • →Otherwise hold cash (T-bill proxy)
  • →10 bps cost per switch

Fails in V-shaped crashes (1987, 2020): sells near the bottom.

Attempt to break it

Every SMA length from 3 to 24 months beat buy-and-hold out-of-sample on Sharpe, and walk-forward selection also beat it. Not broken. Since 1900 it returned slightly more (11.6% vs 10.1%/yr) with far smaller drawdowns — the edge is mostly avoiding a few deep bear markets.

Anti-overfitting

300 random seasonal rules (hold in 6 random calendar months). The 10 best in training look skilled in training; out-of-sample they fall back toward the average. Selection, not skill.

Best 10 · train
0.46
Same 10 · test
0.40
All 300 · test
0.37

Train/test rank correlation: 0.13 — close to zero. Picking winners in-sample predicted almost nothing.

  • Look-ahead bias: every signal is computed at month-end and applied the following month.
  • Survivorship bias: the index includes failed companies as they dropped out — but the stock universe above does not.
  • Data leakage: the 1980 split was fixed before testing; no parameter was tuned on test data.
  • Parameter sensitivity: full grids are shown, not just the winner.

Optimize for robustness, not for an impressive backtest. A rule that only works with one exact parameter is a description of the past, not a strategy.

Problem

Parents of sophomore–senior athletes in football, soccer, basketball, lacrosse, volleyball and baseball who hope to play in college (D1–D3, NAIA, JUCO).

Film 2–3 games with a phone on an auto-tracking gimbal. Cut a 3–4 minute reel with the athlete's best plays first, spotlight arrows, stats overlay and contact card. Add a one-page web profile (measurables, GPA, schedule, video) and a coach-email template list.

Red team: the top three

Each one attacked as hard as possible, then improved.

Recruit Reel

Chosen
Why would customers refuse?
Free tools exist (phone + editing apps), and big recruiting services already sell to these families.
Why hasn't this already won?
National services sell software and email blasts, not in-person filming at local games. Local videographers charge $1,000+ and are slow.
Could competitors copy it?
Yes, but the moat is local presence, speed, and a visible portfolio inside each team.
Is the market large enough?
One high school has ~300 varsity athletes; even 5% buying at $449 is about $6.7K per school per year.
Is pricing realistic?
Yes: well under recruiting services ($1K–$4K) and higher-value than a shaky clip.
Can a teenager execute it?
Yes: you're already at games, editing skills are learnable in weeks, and the gear is under $500.
Legal issues
Filming minors needs parent consent; use licensed music; NCAA rules allow third-party highlight videos. Never promise scholarships.
Operational bottleneck
Editing time in peak season. Fix: templates, a standard reel structure, and hiring a second editor.
Killer assumption
Parents will pay before seeing results. Mitigation: free 30-second teaser from the first game.
Improved

Lead with a free teaser, sell the $449 package, and add season updates for recurring revenue. Build a coach-email tracker to prove exposure (opens and replies).

Ref Ready

Why would leagues refuse?
Some assignors already do this as volunteers or through assigning software.
Killer assumption
You can keep enough reliable refs. Teen refs quit mostly because of parent abuse, so mentoring and conduct rules are the product.
Copyable?
Assigning software exists. The moat is your pool of refs and the league relationship.
Legal
Contractor payments, certification requirements and youth work rules. A parent runs payouts.
Improved

Start as a ref yourself, then add scheduling for one league. Charge per filled slot and guarantee coverage with a backup list.

Glow Holiday Lights

Killer assumption
A teen can safely do roof installs. They can't alone: adult handles all elevated work.
Seasonality
90% of revenue in 10 weeks. Fine as a high-earning winter season.
Copyable?
Easily, but stored custom-cut lights create high renewal lock-in.
Legal
Liability insurance and adult ownership required.
Improved

Parent-teen company. Ground-level and single-story homes first; upsell permanent track lighting via an installer partner for referral fees.

12 — Final Business

Recruit Reel

Get seen by college coaches: a recruiting film made at your games, delivered in 72 hours.

RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS
Problem

Most high-school athletes are never seen by college coaches. Recruiting services charge $1,000–$4,000+, and parent-filmed clips are shaky, too long and skip the best plays.

Customer

Parents of sophomore–senior athletes who want to play in college at any level. The athlete is the champion; the parent pays.

Pain

Coaches decide in seconds. A bad reel means no reply, the recruiting window closes junior year, and parents don't know what coaches want to see.

Existing alternatives

National recruiting platforms, team film software, freelance videographers ($800–$2,000), or parents editing phone clips themselves.

Why they fail

Platforms sell software and promises, not a finished film. Freelancers are slow and expensive. Parents lack the footage angles and editing know-how.

FLOW solution

Filmed in person at 2–3 games with an auto-tracking gimbal and cut to the format coaches prefer: best 5 plays first, spotlight markers, stat overlay, contact card. Delivered in 72 hours with a web profile and a coach-email kit.

The money path

  1. Pricing

    Reel $249 · Reel + profile + coach-email kit $449 (core) · Season plan with 4 updates $799.

  2. Revenue model

    One-time packages plus season-update plans; add-ons (extra game $75, rush 24-hour delivery $50, training-session filming $120).

  3. Startup cost

    $350–$700: auto-tracking phone gimbal, tripod, external mic, free editing software (CapCut/DaVinci), $12/yr domain, Google Forms and payment app (parent-held).

  4. First customer

    A teammate: make their reel free, post it (with permission) and ask their parents to share it in the team group chat.

  5. First $100

    One $249 reel for a second teammate after the free sample, in week 2.

  6. First $1,000

    Three core packages ($449 × 3) in the first season, driven by one team.

  7. First $10,000

    ~22 core packages across 3–4 teams and 2 sports in year 1, plus season plans.

  8. First $100,000

    A small studio: 2–3 trained student filmers per school, 6–10 schools, templated editing; you run sales, quality and coach relationships. Requires an LLC and insurance (parent-owned).

Operating it

Team parent meetings, coaches' referrals, a 30-second free teaser of every game you're already at, Instagram/TikTok highlight posts (with consent).
$50 credit per referred family; team-bundle pricing (5+ athletes = 15% off) turns one buyer into a roster.
Season plans; senior-year updates; a 'commitment day' graphic and film when an athlete commits.
Booking form → schedule → upload folder → editing template → auto email with link and invoice. Coach-email tracker shows opens and replies.
Film Friday/Saturday games, edit Sunday–Tuesday, deliver within 72 hours. Standard reel structure keeps edit time near 4 hours.
Phone, auto-tracking gimbal, tripod, mic, laptop, editing software, cloud storage, simple website.
Holds the payment account and any contracts, signs off on pricing, drives to away games, owns the LLC if it grows.
Written parent consent to film minors; respect venue filming rules; licensed music only; NCAA permits third-party highlight video, so never promise scholarships or act as an agent.
Peak-season editing crunch, venue restrictions, quality inconsistency as you add filmers, and families expecting guaranteed offers.
Present at the game, fast, affordable, and built to what coaches actually watch. Every finished reel advertises the next one inside the team.

Plan

  1. 30-day plan

    Make 3 free reels, build the site, post samples, pitch 2 coaches, sell the first 2 paid packages.

  2. 90-day plan

    10 paid packages, team-bundle deals with 2 teams, a templated workflow under 4 hours per reel, and 5 testimonials.

  3. 1-year vision

    Go-to recruiting film service for 3–4 schools across 2–3 sports; ~$10K revenue; one trained second filmer.

  4. Long-term vision

    A network of student filmers across the region using the Recruit Reel template, with a recruiting dashboard that tracks coach engagement for every athlete.

13 — Red Team

Attack everything.

The strongest objection to each conclusion on this page — and what would prove it wrong.

Strongest objection
Scores are one analyst's judgment from mid-2026 knowledge; prices have moved since. The ranking is not point-in-time and cannot be backtested.
Failure condition
Top-ranked names underperform the equal-weight universe over 12–24 months.
Evidence that would invalidate it
A blind re-score by a second source disagreeing on >40% of the top 10.
What should change
Refresh metrics from filings each quarter; log every score change with a reason.
Strongest objection
High-win-rate dip-buying (pullback, multi-factor) decayed: profit factor fell below 1 after 2005. Only trend-following held, on just 29 trades.
Failure condition
Trend whipsaw years in range-bound oil.
Evidence that would invalidate it
Running the same rules on 20+ liquid stocks and finding no edge.
What should change
Re-test on equity daily data with volume when available. Treat WTI results as illustrative.
Strongest objection
Trend following's edge is mostly drawdown avoidance from a few events (1929–32, 1973–74, 2000–02, 2008). Few independent episodes = weak statistics.
Failure condition
A fast crash and rebound (1987, 2020) — the rule sells low and buys back higher.
Evidence that would invalidate it
Out-of-sample Sharpe falling below buy-and-hold over a full cycle (currently 0.89 vs 0.63).
What should change
Prefer partial de-risking (50%) over all-or-nothing switching to reduce whipsaw cost.
Strongest objection
Scenario returns are judgment, scenario weights are assumptions, and holdings are correlated (AI capex). Bear cases will arrive together.
Failure condition
AI capex cycle turns: GROWTH/AGGRESSIVE bear cases realized simultaneously.
Evidence that would invalidate it
Correlation of holdings > 0.7 in a drawdown.
What should change
Cap total AI-capex exposure; keep the T-bill sleeve; size AGGRESSIVE as a small satellite only.
Strongest objection
Recruit Reel sells hope. Families may expect scholarships, and national recruiting platforms already market heavily to them.
Failure condition
Fewer than 5 paid packages after one full season of filming.
Evidence that would invalidate it
Parents watch the free teaser but don't buy, or coaches never open the reel links.
What should change
Sell exposure, not outcomes. Track coach opens and replies to prove value, and lead with team bundles.
Strongest objection
EXTREME's score correlates 0.64 with momentum alone — partly a momentum screen. Neither formula has a stock-level out-of-sample test.
Failure condition
EXTREME top names fall >50% in a rate shock.
Evidence that would invalidate it
A point-in-time backtest showing no excess return vs. equal weight.
What should change
Collect point-in-time scores quarterly starting now — build the out-of-sample record forward.
Strongest objection
FLOW DIVERGENCE was mostly the trend rule in disguise.
Failure condition
Already failed: no out-of-sample improvement.
Evidence that would invalidate it
Shown in the FLOW Investing Lab below.
What should change
Rejected at index level. Next experiment: stock-level estimate revisions vs. price stress.

14 — FLOW Formulas

Two formulas. Opposite jobs.

FLOW EXTREME hunts asymmetric upside and accepts brutal drawdowns. FLOW CORE compounds while avoiding ruin. CORE is not a weaker EXTREME — their rankings are negatively correlated.

RESEARCH HYPOTHESISRank correlation EXTREME vs CORE: -0.27 · shared top-10 names: 2
Super-risky

FLOW EXTREME

E = 0.25·Growth + 0.25·Optionality + 0.20·Momentum + 0.15·ExpectationGap + 0.15·Catalyst (gate: BalanceSheet ≥ 5)

Top 8 by score, weight ∝ score, cap 20% per name, kill rule: exit at −35% from entry or on thesis invalidation.

  • ·Momentum has the longest documented record of any return anomaly (≈ 1927–present, many countries) — kept at 20%, not more, because momentum crashes after bear markets.
  • ·Growth and optionality drive the right tail (5–10×) that this formula exists to capture.
  • ·Expectation gap and catalysts make the upside time-bound instead of hope-based.
  • ·Valuation is deliberately excluded — it is the main thing EXTREME is willing to pay for; it reappears as a risk, not a score.
Current top 10
RKLBGOOGLAMDPLTRNVDAIONQVRTMULLYAVGO
Less-risky

FLOW CORE

C = 0.30·Quality + 0.20·BalanceSheet + 0.15·Valuation + 0.15·(10 − Volatility) + 0.10·Growth + 0.10·Momentum × Market-trend overlay

Top 12, equal weight, max 12% per name, max 30% per sector, rebalance quarterly. When the S&P 500 closes a month below its 10-month average, cut equity to 50% and hold T-bills (tested 1900–2026, walk-forward validated).

  • ·Profitability/quality and low volatility are documented, persistent factors (Novy-Marx 2013; Frazzini–Pedersen 2014).
  • ·Balance sheet strength reduces permanent loss in recessions.
  • ·Valuation kept small (15%): our own test showed valuation timing failed out of sample at the index level; it still prevents overpaying.
  • ·The trend overlay is the one component with a real out-of-sample result in FLOW's own backtests.

New frameworkRESEARCH HYPOTHESIS

FLOW DIVERGENCE

Stress–Fundamental Divergence

Prices and fundamentals are coupled with a lag. When fear pushes price down while fundamentals are still improving, forward returns should be high; when price AND fundamentals break together, risk dominates.

Most frameworks look at price OR fundamentals. FLOW DIVERGENCE trades the disagreement between them — the moment investor psychology decouples from business reality.

DD_t = P_t / max(P_≤t) − 1 (stress: how far below the peak)
ΔE_t = E_t / E_{t−12} − 1 (fundamental direction: trailing earnings growth)
Trend_t = 1[P_t > SMA10_t]
w_t = Trend_t; override w_t = 1 if DD_t ≤ θ and ΔE_t > 0 (stress + healthy fundamentals); force w_t = 0 if Trend_t = 0 and ΔE_t < 0 (both broken)
Decided at month-end t, applied in t+1 (no look-ahead). θ = −10%.
Inputs
  • Price drawdown from peak
  • Trailing 12-month earnings growth
  • 10-month moving average
  • (v2) Earnings yield − 10Y yield vs its 20-year median
Decision rules
  • Default: follow the trend.
  • Divergence buy: price ≥10% off highs while earnings still growing → stay invested.
  • Confirmation sell: below trend AND earnings falling → cash.
Risk controls
  • Max 1 switch per month
  • 10 bps cost per switch
  • No leverage
Exit conditions
  • Earnings growth turns negative while below trend
  • Drawdown recovers above trend (override no longer needed)
Failure conditions
  • Earnings data lags (reported quarterly, revised) — the 'healthy fundamentals' you see may already be stale.
  • Crises where earnings fall after prices (2008): the override keeps you in too long.
Potential advantages
  • Intuitive, few parameters
  • Combines psychology (stress) with fundamentals
Potential disadvantages
  • Needs timely earnings data
  • Mostly overlaps with trend following
Portfolio

Index-level: 100% equities or 100% T-bills. Stock-level version (untested): rank stocks by drawdown × positive estimate revisions. Rebalancing: Monthly, at month-end close.

Average next-12-month S&P return by state — does the core claim hold in both periods?
State1900–19791980–2023
Stress + healthy earnings (drawdown <= -10%, EPS growth > 0)5.5% · 326 mo13.7% · 113 mo
Stress + falling earnings (drawdown <= -10%, EPS growth < 0)8.9% · 268 mo5.3% · 57 mo
Calm + healthy earnings2.0% · 269 mo8.6% · 217 mo
Calm + falling earnings9.3% · 94 mo11.3% · 128 mo
Is it actually different?
Barely. 86% of months had the same position as the 10-month trend rule.
Is it secretly an existing factor?
Yes — mostly time-series momentum/trend, with a valuation-ish tilt in v2.
Is it overfit?
θ sensitivity was flat (test Sharpe 0.77–0.90 across −5% to −30%), so not fragile — just not better.
Does hindsight create the edge?
The 1980–2023 'stress + healthy earnings' 98% hit rate is hindsight-prone: few independent episodes (≈5 bear markets).
Do costs destroy it?
No — ~1 switch/year; costs are small.
Multiple periods?
Conditional forward returns flipped between periods. Fails.
Multiple regimes?
Helps in slow bear markets, hurts in fast earnings-led crashes.
Out-of-sample?
Not better than the simpler rule.
Overly complex?
Yes relative to its value.
Explained by something simpler?
Yes: the 10-month trend rule.

Verdict — REJECTED (as a new edge). v1 behaved 86% like plain trend following (return correlation 0.87) and did not beat it out-of-sample (Sharpe 0.83 vs 0.84). The 'stress + healthy earnings' state was the WORST stress state in 1900–1979 and the best in 1980–2023 — an unstable relationship, not a law. v2 (equity-risk-premium gate) was worse than trend (0.75 vs 0.89). FLOW did not force a success.

FLOW

An Experiment in Better Investing

The idea

Edges live where human behavior forces prices away from reality — but the simplest description of that behavior (trend) already captures most of it at the index level.

The method

Hypothesis → rules → 126 years of data → train/test split → walk-forward → parameter sensitivity → red team → accept/reject. Failed ideas are kept.

The evidence

Trend following was the only index rule that survived every test: OOS Sharpe 0.89 vs 0.63, max drawdown −19% vs −49%, every parameter from 3–24 months beat buy-and-hold OOS, walk-forward Sharpe 0.77 vs 0.50 since 1920. Its gain is risk control, not higher returns.

The weaknesses

Monthly index data only; no point-in-time stock fundamentals; few independent bear markets; dividends frozen after 2023; WTI used as swing proxy.

The next experiment

Test FLOW DIVERGENCE at the STOCK level with point-in-time analyst estimate revisions (price drawdown × upward revisions), where the disagreement between price and fundamentals is far more frequent than at index level.

Research quality

Fetch once, cache in research/raw, recompute locally. Refresh only market snapshot data when stale (>30 days).

Bias controls
Signals lagged one period; train/test split at 1980; walk-forward; parameter grids reported in full; costs included; failed experiments kept (4 index strategies rejected).
